topic: 3 signs your back pain is probably not serious

slides.headline: Back's gone. Should you panic?
slides.sub: Three signs it's the common, settles-on-its-own kind.

slides.title: First, the reassuring bit
slides.body: The vast majority of back pain, even the kind that stops you standing up straight, is not a sign of damage. It's painful, it's scary, and it usually settles within a few weeks.

slides.title: Sign 1: it came on with a movement
slides.body: Bent to pick something up, twisted in the garden, sneezed. A clear moment it started, with no other symptoms, is the classic pattern for a strain that will calm down.

slides.title: Sign 2: it changes with position
slides.body: Worse sitting, better walking. Or the other way round. Pain that shifts with how you move is mechanical, and mechanical pain responds well to movement and time.

slides.title: Sign 3: it stays in the back
slides.body: Pain that sits across the lower back, maybe into one buttock, without pins and needles or weakness in the legs, is very rarely something that needs a scan.

slides.title: The few things that do need a check
slides.body: Numbness around the groin, trouble controlling bladder or bowel, leg weakness that's getting worse, fever, or pain after a serious fall. These are uncommon, but don't wait on them.

slides.headline: Want a plan, not a scan?
slides.body: Our physios assess what's driving it, get you moving safely on day one and give you a short routine that speeds things up. Chatswood and Sydney CBD.

caption:
Back's gone. Should you panic? Probably not. 🙂

Most back pain, even the kind that has you shuffling to the car, is not damage. Three signs it's the common kind: it started with a movement (lifting, twisting, sneezing), it changes with position, and it stays in the back and buttock without pins and needles or weakness in the legs. That pattern responds to movement, reassurance and time, and scans rarely change the plan.

A few things do need checking promptly: numbness around the groin, bladder or bowel changes, leg weakness that's getting worse, fever, or pain after a serious fall. Uncommon, but worth knowing.
